p:
So thank you, Council Member. I will just start by saying, um, Shannon Midelton, uh, who is my new First Deputy Commissioner, is also our Chief Savings Officer and also our former Chief Financial Officer. So she's wearing 3 hats here today, um, and I will be, um, uh, giving her the opportunity to give a lot of numbers to you. Um, that's why her budget is thicker than my— I mean, her binder is thicker than mine. Um, so as you noted, we are, um, working towards the March 20th deadline. So unfortunately, it is sort of tricky for us to be able to, um, bring you some of the ideas that we're already working on, but we are working on ideas right now. Um, and I think we feel, um, you know, as, as an agency that has a lot of opportunities to generate revenue and find savings through creative means, um, through our procurement and other mechanisms, I think we're, um, cautiously optimistic that we'll be able to, um, help the city

and this current fiscal, fiscal circumstance. I don't know if you wanna add anything.
No, I think you covered it. We're looking at our strength—
Please speak into the mic.

Sorry. The Commissioner covered it. We're looking to leverage our strength as a buyer in procurement and how we can look to deliver those services, um, more efficiently and cheaper for all other city agencies, not just for
And how many vacancies do you have? Because that could be impacted.
Yes. So our total vacancies is 370 as of January, and that's about a 15% vacancy rate.
Okay. I guess that could be used as part of it, but—
Correct.

Ah, hmm. How does DCAS assess which vehicle models and brands are the best suited for city operations? This is all about the city electric vehicles. How do you measure reliability and efficiency and longevity of what you purchase? Are there, uh, factors such as range, charge times, the

battery mileage taken into consideration? And of course, I read in the papers, you know more than I do, that, you know, that guy in the White House is scaling back, uh, electric, which is obviously a mistake in our opinion, and I'm sure in yours. But how does the production, uh, or manufacturing, how is it impacted by federal, um, standards? And has this posed any difficulties to procure um, and then I have more questions. You do have a really great guy who runs your fleet.
Yes, I think his name is Keith. No, um, so-
We know him very well, we love him. Go ahead.
Yes. So um, I'm gonna have, uh, Deputy Commissioner Kerman answer this question because, uh, there's a lot of technical pieces to this that I think he can, um, help bring detail to.
Okay, Keith Kerman, Chief Fleet Officer. Good to see you again, um, Council Member.
Nice to see you.

So one, you know, we work with the agencies to specify all the different vehicles. The city has an unbelievably complicated fleet, 120

on-road models, 70 off-road. We're really running hundreds and hundreds of different service operations, you know, so when we say it's a fleet, but it's a pretty complicated thing. We work with agencies on the specifications, including for electric vehicles. Um, we continue to be, um, all in on electrification. Um, and, and we've made a lot of progress. You know, just 3 years ago, I could not have told you that we had a single all-electric pickup or van. We're operating 800 now and growing that fleet and very popular vehicles working tremendously. We've introduced our first electric garbage trucks, um, non-plowing units, our first electric box trucks, our first electric sweepers, our first electric rack trucks and, and many other models. We're working with NYBD. We just introduced the first pursuit-rated, police-rated, all-electric vehicle, the Chevy Blazer EV, and NYBD has their first 50 units and are testing them now. Uh, there's a lot of proof that has to go into that kind of transition. Um, so we're, we're continuing to, to be all in. There's no question that federal policy has led to some announcements recently. You know, we

really were a big adopter of the Ford Lightning, the pickup truck, and that's gonna go off the market at least for a short. Um, but we do have another EV model, um, that is available. Um, we are the largest national user of the Chevy Bolt and so there's gonna be a short period left that we can get the Bolt. We're gonna try and get as many as we can. Um, but right now we have not, you know, we read the news too, and, and these models, and we are talking to manufacturers constantly.
They're still manufacturing electric? Because I—
Absolutely.
If you read the papers, you'd think not.

No, correct. That's not true. No part of our program has stopped. Have we lost a few vehicle models? Yes, but we have other models to replace them. Are we concerned about the supply chain? Of course, we're, we're out there. But I will say that DCAS is doing everything possible to advocate for electric vehicles. To partner with other cities, with other jurisdictions, and we hope to say a lot more about that in just the next couple months

to make sure that we keep the pressure on. EV hybrids are unbelievably efficient. You, you, you mentioned efficiency. We just published our Local Law 75 use-based fuel economy report. We thank you for that. Um, going back, I, I think about 15 years. Electric vehicles are incredibly efficient, 9 times more efficient than combustion vehicles. If you care about efficiency, then electrifying your transport is what you would do. Um, we— a plug-in hybrid is more efficient than a hybrid. Or I, I should go, an EV is more efficient than a plug-in hybrid. A plug-in hybrid's more efficient than a hybrid, and a hybrid is way more efficient than a gas. Everything in the electrification, we are achieving efficiency, and we just published that report. So, um, you know, we are still all in. We think these are the smart investments. Save enormously on fuel and emissions, but they also save enormously on maintenance. 60 to 70% fewer breakdowns, less maintenance costs. So you are saving on these vehicles, not just reducing pollution, but they're smart, efficient investments. And, you know, we're concerned about the

marketplace, but we'll do our best to influence it and so far, everything moves forward.

Okay, that's helpful because when you listen to the, um, Press, you hear differently. Now, um, I think your deadline is 2035. What does that deadline, uh, mean? No, what, what do you— what deadline do you have to supposedly, depending on the manufacturing situation, to be electric all the way?
So-
Oh, go ahead.
Uh, so Local Law 140 requires the light and medium duty vehicles of the city to be electric by 2035.
Right.
And then the heavy and specialized and emergency by 2038.
Okay.
If doable.
Right.

On the, you know, on the main, uh, er, light and medium duty vehicles, your pickups, your, your vans, your SUVs, your sedans, you know,

today there are models out there and we can implement and we're moving forward. There's no question that when you get into things like obviously plow trucks, we just went through a big storm emergency. There is not an electric viable plow truck on the planet Earth today. So that we have to see, right? We're talking to manufacturers. We're gonna— if we can push it and achieve it, we will but, you know, we have to be realistic. There are limitations.
We have to be realistic based on the federal situation too.
As well, right? Certainly, you know, our ability to implement electric models depends on further investment in the industry. It depends on further development in the industry.
Okay.

Um, but we are moving forward in 2035 for light and medium would be that first big target. There's a lot more opportunity to electrify the light and medium side than when you get into plow trucks, some of our fire trucks and ladders-
Right.
Where there's a lot more complication operationally.

Okay. Now, how much funding do you have from OMB to purchase? In other words, are you— can you get as many as you want? Do you have a, you know, maybe, I don't know, 200-something that you're funded for and you need another 500? How, how does the funding work? Because of course, I mean, I think, you know, everybody would love to be able to buy everything tomorrow, but I didn't know if that's a challenge.
So currently in our Expense Budget, we have $10 million every Fiscal Year. Um, and in our Capital Budget, just in Fiscal Year '26, we have $7.8 million.
Okay.
Now that supports— that $10 million supports roughly 220 vehicles a year. I think in order to hit the numbers we need to by 2035, on average, we should probably be doing around 640, uh, vehicles.
640 per, per year, okay. And now it’s 222 or something like that.
Yes and we're in conversations with OMB continuing.

Okay, well we need to make sure— we've been joined by Council Member Lee and Council Member Hankerson. Thank you both for being here. Okay, the other question I have is, um, I know this sounds silly, but my, um, city store, how much revenue have you generated I guess, in '26, um, and how is this revenue utilized?
Thank you, Council Member. Yes, I'm going to turn that to my numbers person.

Yes, so we're happy to report, um, in Fiscal Year '25, our revenue increased, um, from $387,000 in Fiscal Year '24 to $463,000. So we've definitely seen, you know, the impact of the beautification, the renovations, and the highlighting um, of the city store. That's a revenue that goes to support the general fund and help— helps the city close the gap, um, similar to all other DCAS revenue streams. Um, yeah.

Okay. Um, and then the auto auction contract with GovDeals. Why was a new contract required and what factors were considered

with this vendor? Was there an issue with the prior one? And then how long is this contract with GovDeals?
Okay.
This is on the auction end, yeah.

Sure, so, um, we had a vendor, IAA. We've been doing online auctions, as you know, since 2012, and that in general has been very successful and grown our market to really a national market. Um, but we did default the vendor IAA, um, and we went through a long process with them. At the most basic, they were not providing the full level of public access to these auctions that was required in the contract. And we tried to resolve this issue with them, but were unable to do so. Um, we've gone to GovDeals and the good news, we do not have a public access issue and we've got about 40% more revenue per vehicle coming in. Those issues kind of being tied together. So we are in a good place right now. We're having a very, very strong auction year in Fiscal Year '26. We will far exceed our target. Um, and we're seeing much more return in a much more vibrant market.

So we did what we had to do to move that vendor, um, uh, to change the vendor, but we are in a strong place now.
How long is that contract for? Gov—
The current GovDeals contract? I would need to check on the terms for that.

Okay, I think you talked about this issue, but to meet the city's renewable energy goals and achieve Local Law 97, because that's what -not only does the city have to do it, but the private sector, they always calling me. Um, do you have adequate resources to reduce the emissions from government operations by 50% by 2030? Which of course is— I know you talked about it a little bit, but can you be more— This is a huge question from the community.

Yes, thank you, Council Member and I just want to say, you know, I, I acknowledge that, um, uh, that we have more to do. Um, this issue, even mandates aside, I think as, as we've sort of discussed on with my team, you know, I think even if and when we exceed targets, there's still going to be more to do because this is such an existential issue.

And, um, that's why we're working very aggressively every year to deliver projects that reduce our emissions. Um, I am, um, pleased to say that we are on track to, um, with our, with our current funding, to, um, to exceed, um, our targets, um, by 2030.
Okay, and why do you think that's possible? Just because you have the funding or you have already good infrastructure or—

So yeah, so, so it's, it's a combination of things. One is, um, a large number of projects to reduce our emissions, um, which, uh, we can— we're happy to go into greater detail if that's helpful. Um, and then the other thing is that we're bringing online, um, uh, er, a large, um, project that will be delivering, um, clean power, uh, via Hydro-Québec, um, bringing down, um, hydropower from Canada. Um, uh, er, and it'll be about 20% of New York City's electricity and 100% of all of New York City government's electricity.
Huh, okay. Is there anything you wanna add to that? Cause any other aspect to it? In other words, you really feel that you're gonna get to that point? Okay.
Yes, that's coming online this— I'm scooping myself a little. That's coming on online this year.
Okay, alright. Um, DCAS, do you gonna— we're all talking about Rikers Island. I, I assume it closes.
Yes.

And then I assume the Renewable Rikers Act of 2021 will go into effect. Um, and obviously we want it to be a sustainable situation. Do you have resources and a timeline to complete a master plan, um, to, uh, design and build this new infrastructure? I think we're talking about wastewater closing for plants, as I understand it, and then moving them, and then there's much more. So I just didn't know where you are in those plants. Of course, the facilities, borough-based, are not even built yet.

Right. Yes, it is a little bit, um, it is, it is a little bit in the future. Um, and, uh, you know, obviously we're, um, we've, we've already been sort of in the past Administration has already been sort of thinking about that. Um, we, um, with the changeover of the Administration, um, obviously

there's new appointments that had to be made for that um, Committee that meets, um, which we participate in. Um, so, um, we'll be, um, uh, resetting that soon, but, um, uh, you know, it is a little bit in the future right now, so I would say that the plans are not, uh, not yet at the stage where, um, things are fully fleshed out.
Yeah, I mean, it's a huge program to plan for, so hopefully—

Yes, but we're, you know, I mean, any opportunity I think that we have to build, um, solar or any other, um, uh, infrastructure for, um, reducing our emissions is obviously an exciting opportunity for us.

Okay. Now, the hottest summer days are not here, but when they do arrive, the Energy Demand Management Program, which reduces pollution, reduces energy costs, and saves public agencies obviously money on the hottest days, uh, the data shows that DCAS has energy savings and revenue generated by the program have plateaued in recent years. So my question is, do you have the resources

to expand this successful energy demand management program? But particularly in the summer, obviously.
So you're talking about our demand response program, right?
I am, yup.
Yeah.
I mean, how's it going basically is what I'm trying to say.

Yes and first of all, I would just like to say it feels like we are exercising our demand response in this room right now. Um, uh, but, um, yes, we're definitely obviously thinking about all options about how to expand, um, you know, our, our ways to save energy through demand response. Um, I don't know if you wanna add anything to that.

Yep um, on the resource side, um, it, it fluctuates, right? Because it's based on the weather, it's based on peak usage. Um, but we have been seeing solidly at least $2 million, um, every fiscal year. And we use that revenue to reinvest into our buildings and create more energy efficiency, um, upgraded, uh, equipment.
So $2 million savings is what you're saying?
Um, revenue, yes.
Too much revenue.
Revenue, yep.
Okay, alright I, I hope that works. Uh, can't— we've been joined. Go ahead. You wanna add something? Go ahead.

Oh, now we are. Uh, and this is a citywide revenue program too. So we, we are, we have grown over the past few years in terms of citywide revenue led by our energy supply team and, uh, we are expecting it. We have enrolled the highest number of facilities in program history right now. So we are expecting it to continue to grow.

Okay and this includes, I mean, I, I don't sort of an aside, but I am always concerned and hopeful for the CIGs, Cultural Institution Groups, and that they're in this pile of being better managed for all of these above reasons. So you only, you manage those that are power and light, right? Is that something that DCAS is involved with? I think you are.
Um, could you repeat the question?
Sure, the, the, CIGs, which are the—
Their enrollment in demand response?
Yes.
Um, only enrollees who are able to meet the requirements of the program are enrolled.
Okay, it depends then.
Yeah, the, the facility has to confirm ahead of time that they are able to meet their obligation.
Okay.
During that period of peak load, if they can, they're enrolled.
Okay.
And there, it's never going to be a continuity of service issue.

Okay, the reason I ask is we're always trying to make sure they get saved because they have so many cuts. Yeah and they're barely surviving with the federal cuts. Um, Council Member Zhuang has joined us, and, uh, Chair Lee, you have some questions.

Hi, good afternoon. Um, and it's great to see you, Commissioner. I feel like it's

been a lifetime since we last interacted when I was at
Oh yeah.

Ah, yes. Um, so just really quickly, um, in terms of the Space Savings Initiative, um, throughout various plans we have seen several adjustments to account for various space savings initiatives, and, uh, they aim to make better use of the city's owned and leased spaces to reduce costs. And just wanted to know how much did the city save from space savings initiatives in FY25, and how much has been saved to date in FY26?

I just want to note, um, on the space savings, uh, obviously there's been a tremendous amount of work that has b-been done to survey all all of the agencies, and that's one of the things that I'm really excited to dig into because I think there's a lot of potential there. But, um, we have already started to do some of that work, so I'll, I'll give it to, uh, the First Deputy Commissioner to sort of add the numbers here.

Thank you, Commissioner. Um, so Fiscal Year '25 was a big planning year, um, getting the surveys out, identifying, um, agency space usage

needs. Um, in Fiscal Year '26, um, year to date, we've already realized almost $8 million, and that's a combination of cost avoidance as well as actual savings to the lease budget.
Perfect and, um, do you keep a record of which agencies, uh, are sharing spaces? And is this publicly reported anywhere that we can access?
Um, we'll have our DC of— our EDC of real estate and facilities management.

Good morning. Thank you for that question. So it's not currently publicly reported except that our— all of our lease data is available, uh, online and, and that is publicly reported. So you would be able to, you know, eventually see, uh, lease reductions where we're vacating a space entirely. Uh, but some examples are, um, the Law Department consolidated some of its space at 100 Church Street and we were able to move the Campaign Finance Board out of another lease site into that site, thereby relinquishing space at 80 Main and Lane. Um, another example is HRA consolidating out of, uh, 404 Pine or Department of Finance, um, consolidating into one of

their other sites so HRO could move into their vacated site. So that's just some examples of how we got to those numbers.
Perfect. Um, and how do you determine which agencies would be best suited to share space? Is there some kind of survey or—
Um, we persuade them nicely.
I'm sorry?
We persuade them nicely. I mean, I mean, it really works.

Well, I was just gonna say, I mean, I think the general process as we're sort of, um, as people's leases come up and stuff like that, we look at a case-by-case basis and what the agency's needs are, and we, um, think about like where we can actually put them. And at that point, you know, because there's a little bit of a moving target as we're sort of doing each of these moves because, um, you know, the space, the space evolves as people- as you know, from being in an agency, the space evolves as people sort of have moved from one space to another.

So we're constantly refining and having conversations with the agencies about their needs, and then we'll figure out where we can fit people. But our number one goal, obviously, is to make sure that we're being responsible with the taxpayer dollars and, um, you know, also making sure that agencies have adequate space to work in.
Perfect, thank you. Um, and just moving on to Con Edison Smart Charge and other adjustments I say this as someone who drives an EV car, full EV, and selfishly I have a question because-
I want to— she wants a charging station at City Hall Park.

No, but you know what's crazy is that I asked if I could charge here and I was told no because I'm technically not a city vehicle, but I would gladly pay if I was like in some kind of emergency situation. So I'm just wondering if we're allowed to charge at City Hall.
She’s been asking this since the day she started.
Yeah, exactly.

I will just say, um, we are very aggressively expanding our charging infrastructure. And in fact, one of the things that I like to, um, brag about early and often is that DCAS is— has the largest, uh, charging infrastructure in the state. Um, and, uh, er, along with DOT. Um, and, um, we are constantly looking for places to install, um, charging, not just for city fleet, but we also are now, um, starting to install public, um, charging places. Um, so we are very eager if you have any sites in your district that you think might be a viable option, obviously tell us.
One at City Hall.
Yes, I'll let, I'll let Keith speak to that specific location.

Yeah, and just to add really quickly, I can recommend places because we're a transit desert in Eastern Queens, and so there's no trains or subways or Long Island Railroads. And so this is something that the community would love.

That would be great. Yeah, and I mean, I think the— obviously there, there are certain criteria that you have to sort of look for in terms of like the electric grid, um, and that's something

that we work closely with Con Ed on. But, um, I don't know, Keith, if you wanted to add anything.

Sure. So the first, the good news, we have a workplace charging initiative. City Hall is in it. We can work out right after this meeting for you to charge. You will have to pay because it is your personal car. But that done, we will have you set up before the end of the day or as soon as we are in touch with you. And then, yeah, we are very open to ideas about additional charging. You know, finding space is the challenge for us. We are in the field every single day with Con Ed assessing locations. If it's viable at a logistics level, right, you gotta have access. And of course, there's got to have juice. We have to have available electric but if you provide us with lists, we can be out there, you know, very soon and in assessing those locations.

Perfect um, and then just more going to the budget piece of this, uh, the Smart Charge. I know the Preliminary Plan includes an additional $1.2 million in other categorical funding for FY26. Only for incentive revenue received for the city's participation in the program. And so how does

Con Ed determine the incentive funding and what types of services and activities are considered?
Keith, you're their most popular guest star.
Yes.

Uh, hmm, so Con Ed has been a really important partner for us and they have the Smart Charge, but then the Ready Charge is actually the big one for us. And so they are providing for every one of the electric chargers that we're installing and just for background, we run the largest, like, fast charging electric network in New York State. We have 415 fast chargers. We are installing more fast chargers literally every single week. So they're providing an offset based not on the pedestal, not on the unit, but based on the electrical upgrades or the electrical costs and those are extraordinarily important funds for us, and we are using those to reinvest uh, that's actually how we do Level 2 chargers. So the slow charger, the overnight charger, most of that is funded through Con Ed grants.

It's also how consistent with Local Law 140, we train mechanics and city fleet operators, um, to really learn about EV and understand how to operate and maintain EV. So the Con Ed partnership has been very important and it really is a daily thing. We are in the field with Con Ed today and every day. And, and what— are there any limitations in terms of how you can utilize the funds once they come back?

I don't believe there is a limitation. I do believe it comes in as general purpose, um, grant funding because it is an offset to expenditures but the reality is how we do in fact use it is to reinvest in our sustainability program. Right. Um, and have you assessed ways to increase participation in the program by city agencies to increase the incentive revenues from Con Ed?
So on the smart charge, yes. So we do have a smart charge program. It involves incentivizing you for basically off-peak charging.
Uhm, mmm.

And so we do that with all our non-emergency agencies where we can. Right? So there are some agencies, you know, I, I, I can't restrict

the charging of police electric cars and other emergency response vehicles. We have to give them flexibility. But certainly, say, at the Parks Department and DEP where you can charge overnight, we are doing that and we are bringing in a revenue stream. As you noted, we are bringing in that smart charge revenue, revenue stream.

Okay and I just have one quick question Chair, if that's okay, on Local Law 97. Um, only because this is a law that really impacts my district heavily because I, despite what people may think, I actually have the most number of co-ops and condos in my area. And so I bring this up to say that there's a bill— there's a couple bills we have that are sort of making adjustments. I know it's probably different for you all because you're, um, city buildings, but, um, the— based on what I'm understanding, the Governor and the State Comptroller themselves have come out with reports basically saying that the grid's not going to be ready in time. And so we're trying to figure out a way, um, at least on the constituency side and the residential side, how to not have the penalties be exorbitant?

Because I know in 2030, um, that's really when the higher fines are going to start and so, if there's a bill in place that we have that literally just matches, uh, the penalties and fees to when the grid will actually be ready, um, is that something that would be helpful, or is it something that would—

I think from, uh, DCAS's perspective You know, we, I think, feel not only are we mandated, but we have a moral obligation to, to move as fast as we can on this. Um, and as, um, uh, you know, as I was sort of referring to earlier when we were doing Q&A, we do have, um, this large source of hydropower that's coming online soon, which will actually allow DCAS to, um, to allow the city to, to meet the targets. So, um, uh, and exceed, I, I should say. And, and also we are very aggressively working on all of the these projects to reduce our consumption. So I don't think that, um, I think for, for, for us, um, even, you know, mandates aside, we want to do as much as possible.

Hmm, mmm, no and I totally get that and I think it's just challenging for— I, I get, and it's good that on the city side you feel

very confident that you can meet those goals. I think the other issue just goes on beyond the, you know, city buildings and where we land with that. So I just wanted to get your thoughts on that, but that's good to hear. So thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you, Chair.
Thank you very much. Uh, Council Member Hankerson.

Thank you, Chair. Uh, I just have a couple of questions, um, regarding some of the recruitment strategies, um, that DCAS uses. Uh, what is DCAS doing to attract more applicants for city jobs? If I can start there.

Thank you, Council Member. Um, so this is something that I'm very excited to dig into because I think, um, there's a, there's a lot of strategies that we already do, and then there's more that I think that we can do. But, um, one of the things I'll just say, and then I'll pass it to our Deputy Commissioner, um, to talk, um, in greater detail about the programs that we do have, is sort of even just demystifying what the civil service system is.

Um, 80% of our, um, jobs are civil service jobs. And I think if you ask a normal New Yorker, they probably couldn't tell you what civil service is. Um, so, you know, I think we're having, you know, conversations with, um, the team, uh, including our comms team about, you know, how can we sort of explain to New Yorkers what civil service is and make sure that when tests are posted, um, that, uh, that people actually know about it and not just people who, you know, would normally know about it, but also broader parts of New Yorkers, especially our graduating high school students and our graduating college students. Um, so we just, um, uh, cut a TikTok video— not TikTok video, Instagram video, sorry— with, um, our DEP commissioner, for example, um, to promote one of our, um, engineering, um, intern exams, um, which will be, uh, which, which will hopefully, you know, help us reach sort of a broader audience. So things like that but I'm gonna pass it to Deputy Commissioner Porter because we also have a number of, um, you know, um, ah, Public Service Corps programs and such that, um, also specifically target, um, broader populations.
